catalog_quote: 1.4 STRESS. Contrastive primary word stress /´/ has been noted falling on the ultimate and penultimate syllables: baháw 'leftover food' and báhaw 'to be healed', toqód 'tree stump' and tóqod 'purpose', sabét 'to understand' and sábet 'to discuss'. Primary word stress on the penultimate syllable of a reduplicated root denotes that the reduplication involves a single stress group rather than two stress groups. Secondary word stress then falls on the syllable preceding the syllable with the primary stress. ... 1.5 PRACTICAL ORTHOGRAPHY ... (2) Primary word stress will not be written on the penultimate syllable. It will be written as acute accent on the ultima and as a circumflex when the stress symbol and grave accent occur over the same vowel: /baráto/ barato 'cheap', /sabét/ sabét 'understand', and /sapáq/ sapâ 'water'.

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim with diacritics on p. 25 of the held Miller & Miller 1976 phonology chapter (Rosetta excerpt) and on the same page of the held full SIL scan; the held 1991 Mamanwa Texts Appendix A independently restates 'Word stress is also phonemic'. The deciding source is the standard (and only) reference grammar by the principal fieldworkers. Searches of Glottolog's list, the SIL archive language page, Crossref, ScholarSpace (Lobel 2013) and the SEAlang Zorc archive turned up no later phonology, prosody or instrumental study of Mamanwa; the three open items fetched sources (Zorc notes, Lobel 2013, Miller 1969) are silent on stress and none contradicts LEXICAL (penult ~ final contrast). Only gap: the Millers' own 1964 PSSHR phonemics article, print-only, which would at most refine the descriptive rule. Coding LEXICAL, right-edge two-syllable window, stands; no action needed.

sources.quote: No stress statement (morphology paper); fn. 3 lists the phoneme inventory and refers to Jeanne & Helen Miller, 'Mamanwa Phonemes and Orthography', Philippine Social Sciences and Humanities Review (1964) for the phonology.

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2013. Philippine and North Bornean languages: issues in description, subgrouping, and reconstruction. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa (ScholarSpace 10125/101972).
sources.quote: No statement on Mamanwa stress. Mamanwa forms are cited with accent marks on varying syllables (haó, kanáo, paníi, ijá, duró vs. karíni, ngaríni), consistent with lexical accent but not discussed; the general remark that 'most languages native to Mindanao ... have lost contrastive stress' (p. 287 fn. 3) does not name Mamanwa.
sources.locator: sec. 3.2.6 'Mamanwa', pp. 78-82; sec. 8.2.9 and ch. on Maranao fn. 3 (p. 287) for general remarks on contrastive accent
